turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, both of you. How have you been getting on with the type two diabetes since we added the insulin?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. I don't know, doctor. Bit up and down, and the bus was late, so I'm all flustered.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): No rush. What's been on your mind with it?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The sugars, mostly. I write them down and then I can't read my own writing. Fasting today was one-eighty-something, and after my tea it was two hundred and something — or, hang on, that might've been Tuesday, not yesterday.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The book lives on the microwave. Half of it's blank, if I'm honest. I'm his carer, mornings only.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's helpful to know. Nurse, what did the checks show?
[SEG0007] person_4 (NURSE): Finger-prick was twelve point four millimoles. Blood pressure one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-two, pulse seventy-four. He was chatty, no fuss.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Still on the diabetes tablets alongside the insulin?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin, yeah. A thousand milligrams, morning and night. Those I don't miss.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the insulin — talk me through what you actually inject.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Lantus, at night, twenty-four units — um, I think. Grey pen, though I sometimes squint at the dial.
[SEG0012] person_4 (NURSE): Can I come in there? The letter on the system says insulin glargine, thirty-two units every night. From the hospital clinic.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No — that's, um, that's not right. I do twenty-four. I don't know, doctor, maybe they typed it wrong.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sunday I watched him click it to twenty-four. He won't let me do the injection itself.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'm hearing two doses and I won't pick one. Do you get it in every night?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Not when I'm on earlies. Out the door at five, and I skip it, 'cause I'm scared I'll go funny on the shift. Three days most weeks. Other nights, yes.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Any other diabetes tablets still going?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Gliclazide they stopped. Eighty milligrams, that was. Ages ago, when the insulin got started, and I don't take it now.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or foods, anything like that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are the feet? Numbness, tingling, any sores?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Feet are fine.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the eyes — any blurring, or little black spots?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No blurring. Eyes are alright. The screening, though, I don't know, doctor. Last spring, or the spring before that, and the letter's in a drawer somewhere.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll get that screening date pulled from the records. Are you drinking more than usual, thirsty?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about your energy?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Shattered, if I'm honest. Worse than before. Last few weeks, specially after a late one. I get in and I just sit there.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been nodding off in the chair before tea. That didn't used to happen.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you had the diabetes, as near as you can?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Five-ish years. Don't ask me the month, I don't know.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. Odd pint of a Saturday, that's me. Still full time at the warehouse, shifts.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a quick look at the feet. Pop the socks off when you're ready.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Sorry, there's a hole in this one, I meant to bin them.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Skin's intact, I can't see any cracks or ulcers. Pulses are easy in both feet. The monofilament feels a bit dull on the right big toe, sharper on the left.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the foot he was going on about in bed. Said it was buzzing.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, well, actually, yeah. The right toes go numb and tingly when I'm lying down. A couple of months, I suppose. Daytime it's not there, so I said no, sorry.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to apologise, I'm glad it's out. My impression is the sugars are running higher than we'd like, and this night-time tingling may be early nerve irritation from the diabetes. Provisional only, not a firm label until we see the bloods.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Does that mean the insulin's wrong?

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not necessarily, and I won't change the dose while we've got two different figures. I'll book bloods today: HbA1c, kidney function, and a cholesterol. Nurse, are you able to take those before they go?
[SEG0042] person_4 (NURSE): Yes, I can do them straight after this.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please bring the grey pen and the hospital letter next time. And try not to skip the night dose on early shifts. Have a small snack if you're worried about going low, rather than leaving it out.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. Half four in the morning, my head's not on the insulin, it's on the bus.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have a look at the feet each evening. I'll see you in four weeks with the results. If a sore appears, or the numbness is there all day, come back sooner than that.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll stick the letter with his keys. We'll be there.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Completed finger-prick glucose is supported; type 'laboratory' and requested_by nurse are not stated.
Screening likely occurred, but completion is uncertain and type 'imaging' is not stated.

omissions.text: Insulin glargine/Lantus dose as actually injected was stated by the patient as 24 units at night, while the system letter said 32 units nightly; the recorded medication entry for current insulin omits the patient's stated 24-unit dose.
Patient reports missing the night-time insulin on early shifts about three days most weeks because he is afraid of going low at work.
Negative finding omitted: patient denied numbness, tingling, or sores in the feet when first asked.
Negative finding omitted: patient denied little black spots/floaters in the vision when asked ('Eyes are alright' after being asked about blurring or little black spots).
Symptom incompletely recorded: thirst/polyuria-type symptom was discussed and the patient gave an equivocal answer ('Sometimes, not really') to drinking more than usual/being thirsty.
Examination finding omitted: monofilament sensation was sharper/normal on the left compared with dulled sensation on the right big toe.
Foot symptom context omitted: caregiver reported the right foot had been 'buzzing' in bed.
Investigation workflow omitted: nurse stated the planned bloods could be taken straight after the consultation.
